title: Glue a broken handle back onto a mug lying on its side, holding the mug still while the other hand presses the handle on
instruction: Glue the broken handle back onto the mug lying on its side: hold the mug still with one hand. With the other, take the glue tube and touch its nozzle to both bare patches where the handle broke off, then lay the tube back down. Take the handle and press its two broken ends onto the bare patches, and hold it there without moving until the glue grabs (3 seconds). Then let go of the handle and the mug, and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Mending a broken mug is an everyday repair: the mug is laid on its side so the handle sits flat against it, one hand keeps it from rolling while the other applies the glue and holds the handle in place until the glue sets.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A green self-healing cutting mat with a printed grid, 3 mm thick, from 18 to 47 cm forward and from 20 cm right to 17 cm left of the centre line, fixed. (2) Lying on its side on the mat, a white glazed stoneware mug (0.30 kg) 8.2 cm across and 9.6 cm tall, with 4 mm walls, a navy band by its rim and a red heart printed on it; its axis runs sideways 38.5 cm forward, its middle 5 cm left of the centre line, its mouth to the left and its broken side toward the arms. On that side, level with its axis, two small bare patches of unglazed clay 1.2 cm across, 2.6 cm right of its middle (by the base) and 2.2 cm left of it (by the mouth), show where the handle broke off. The mug rolls when pushed from the side. (3) The broken handle (25 g), a white glazed C 4 cm deep and 5.6 cm long with a navy stripe: two arms 0.8 cm wide and 1 cm tall, 4.8 cm apart, joined by a grip bar; the broken end of each arm is bare clay. It lies flat on the mat 27 cm forward and 10 cm right of the centre line, its broken ends pointing forward. (4) A tube of superglue (20 g), aluminium with a yellow label, 1.5 cm across and 7.3 cm long with its nozzle, cap off, lying on the mat 25 cm forward and 3 cm right of the centre line, nozzle forward; its crimped end keeps it from rolling. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged from the whole trial. A bare patch gets glue when the nozzle's tip comes within 6 mm of its middle (a drop of glue appears on it, and stays). The glue grabs once, with glue on both patches, the handle has been held in a gripper within 6 mm and 10 degrees of where it belongs on the mug, with the mug moving less than 0.8 cm/s and 0.15 rad/s, for 3 s without a break; then the handle is glued on for good. 1.0: the handle glued on, the mug still lying on the mat (its middle at least 2 cm in from the mat's edges) and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start), at the end; 0.5: the handle glued on; 0.25: glue on both bare patches; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the mug and the handle still.
reset_notes: Take the handle off the mug, clean the glue off both bare patches, lay the mug on its side as in the screenshot and put the handle and the glue tube back in their places.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: glue is a rule: a drop appears on a bare patch the nozzle touches, and the handle is fixed to the mug (a fixed joint switches on) once it has been held in place against the still mug long enough, as the scoring describes; superglue takes longer to set in reality. The mug is a 48-sided tube. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
